parts:
Hi,

In order to explore Gaussian process fitting I have tried the stan code in 16.3 stan language user's manual.  However, for a fake data such as y <- x + rnorm (length (x), mean = x, sd = 0.1)
Both during warmup and sampling I received lot of messages such as
Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected becuase of the following issue:
Error in function stan::prob::multi_normal_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Covariance matrixCovariance matrix is not positive definite. Covariance matrix(0,0) is 160637051.56348917:0.

It looks like two chains converged but receiving messages such as this is scary.

Any clues why it is happening?

Linas

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] gp example in stan user manual [Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected...]
parts:
On Feb 20, 2014, at 4:04 PM, Linas Mockus <linasm...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi,
>
> In order to explore Gaussian process fitting I have tried the stan code in 16.3 stan language user's manual. However, for a fake data such as y <- x + rnorm (length (x), mean = x, sd = 0.1)
> Both during warmup and sampling I received lot of messages such as
> Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected becuase of the following issue:
> Error in function stan::prob::multi_normal_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Covariance matrixCovariance matrix is not positive definite. Covariance matrix(0,0) is 160637051.56348917:0.
>
> It looks like two chains converged but receiving messages such as this is scary.
>
> Any clues why it is happening?

Yes, it’s numerical issues with the Hamiltonian simulation that
use a gradient-based approximation to the curvature. With a step size
too large, it goes out of support to non-positive-definite matrices.

It is not a bug or an error — it just results in a Metropolis rejection
of the usual variety and the results are still valid.

We’re going to remove the message in the near future because it’s been
worrying our users and leading them to think there’s someting intrinsically
wrong with the sampler.

- Bob
